1.description: This looks to be an excellent example of an ancient blacksmithing component. The quality of this artifact is quite remarkable, especially given the fissures that seem to run across the exterior.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: You know, it's not uncommon for cracks like these to form on smithing stands that have been exposed to the enormous heat and pressure of sustained use. It's the sign of a successful smith and enviable craftsmanship.

3.name: Gabrielle Benele
3.description: I can tell you've both been neglecting your arcane studies a bit. Don't those cracks remind you of anything? Perhaps some magically-charged Ayleid ruins? This smith likely made enchanted weapons.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: I haven't seen one of these in a while, good find! It's typical for blacksmiths to use decoctions of various metals in their work. The right mixture of ores can strengthen a forged item, much like finding the right balance of flavors in a cooked meal.

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: It's not just about strength, though many may believe so. The addition of differing ores and decoctions can also increase the flexibility of a tool. An important characteristic, unless you want your sword to shatter the first time you hit something.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: Yes, Ugron, strength and flexibility are important, but we're talking about the Ayleids here! Their culture was infused with magic. Their decoctions probably contained elements to enchant their tools and weapons as they forged them.

1.name: Gabrielle Benele
1.description: Leave it to the Ayleids to inscribe even their bracing with runes and enchantments. I can't make out what the markings may have imbued this artefact with. Maybe a blessing of strength or durability on whatever was forged here?

2.name: Gabrielle Benele
2.description: It's the strangest thing. I've been studying the carvings on this bracing, and I still can't make it out. It's non-reactive to any spells I've tried on it. I need to dig deeper. There must be some ancient form of magicka I've overlooked!

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: Don't strain yourself, Gabrielle. The markings aren't runes or enchantments. It's an inscription. It reads: 'To my stalwart smith with love. May your back never ache and your fire never dim.'

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: You really need my help with this? It's an anvil, obviously. Looks decently worn, but from use, rather than time. It's in the Ayleid style, which places it firmly from the First Era. Anything else?

2.name: Amalien
2.description: Good start, but there's more here. The shape of the anvil itself is reminiscent of the Wild Elves. This smith may have had a penchant for imbuing their creations with nature magic. Magical farming tools, maybe?

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Moreover, has anyone noticed how relatively small the anvil is? Its size suggests the smith had a proclivity for forging precision tools like daggers or arrowheads over swords or axes. You can't overlook the details on these things!

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: Now this is truly ancient! First Era, maybe? I can't place what this artefact would be used for. The crescent shape suggests some form of lunar worship, but the material is an unusual metal that's been treated to resemble stone. Very intriguing.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: I practically had to pry this out of Reginus's hands. But it was worth it. There are some notches on the back that suggest this item wasn't an object of worship itself, but part of a larger piece. I suspect it may be a sculpture or art piece.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Finally got a chance to examine this again when Verita wasn't looking. Further analysis suggests this is an Ayleid decoration of some kind. It resembles the ornaments we've found on some of their larger remnants, like their palanquins and staffs.

704.name: Imitation Palanquin Adornment
704.setName: Music Box, Lament for the Path

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: I wish my fingers were as clever as whoever carved this! The fine details on this metal brace indicate a level of diligence and attention to detail that even Ugron could appreciate. Looks to be part of something larger, but I'm not sure what.

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: Reginus wanted me to look at this one. The craftsmanship is apparent, even with age. Looks to me like a miniature carved pillar. It could have something to do with Ayleid tombs or burial customs. More study is needed.

3.name: Gabrielle Benele
3.description: Of course it's miniature, it's a child's toy! Or a novelty item of some sort. Not everything is as serious as Ugron wants it to be. This item broke off at some point long ago. Even so, it would have been an exquisite gift, from all the detail.

705.name: Miniature Mirroretched Brace
705.setName: Music Box, Lament for the Path

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: Few relics survive the eons unscathed. This mirror is no exception, it's got cracks running all over the surface. Still, it would have been a lovely vanity item for some ancient lady's compact. I wonder when it was broken.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: Perhaps the shattering was intentional? A meditation on the perils of vanity and selfishness? There's something about this mirror that doesn't sit right with me. It's cracked, but how have all the pieces stayed together over the years?

3.name: Amalien
3.description: I knew it! I couldn't sleep last night and found myself musing over the mirror. The cracks are intentional! When gently manipulated, the shards can slide together to create a smooth reflective surface. Ayleid craftsmanship never ceases to amaze me.

706.name: Miniature Shattered Cheval
706.setName: Music Box, Lament for the Path

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: The cogs and gears contained inside this base rival anything created by the Dwemer. But the style of the exterior is distinctly Ayleid. It's a conundrum. I need to consult my books and see if the two cultures ever shared their crafting skills.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: I've never seen Ugron so grumpy as when I noticed the tiny metal keys hidden beneath the gears. They're aligned for the gears to hit them, but I'm not sure what will happen when they do. We're still missing something.

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: I haven't seen one of these since I was a child. It's a music box. Amalien was surprisingly astute with the keys, but even her nimble fingers can't get the melody to play. I'm eager to hear whatever ancient song this box contains.

707.name: Bespoke Mirroretched Base
707.setName: Music Box, Lament for the Path

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: Too large to be an earring, too small to be a key. The crystal at the end is clearly worn from touch, and it fits nicely in the hand. This was made to be used and handled, I just don't know what for.

2.name: Gabrielle Benele
2.description: Reginus was right on his second guess. It's a key or trigger of some kind. The teeth at the other end from the crystal certainly make it seem it should lock into place somehow. The Ayleids never cease to surprise me.

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: Gabrielle is spot-on. It's the trigger for a music box. I had one as a child, and it had the same sort of teeth at the end. The crystalcruft ornament is decorative, probably made to complement the overall design of the music box it came from.

708.name: Crystalcruft Shaped Trigger
708.setName: Music Box, Lament for the Path

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: Just a simple wheel made from iron. The outside rim appears smoothed, from years of hands passing over it. Something's off about its weight, however. It seems to change? Inconsistent.

2.name: Gabrielle Benele
2.description: Such a curious little wheel! Reginus is right about its oddly shifting weight. The jade gem holds a simple magic: when someone spins this wheel, it stays in motion until stopped. Who would need such a thing?

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: You should use your hands for more than holding books, Gabrielle. Such a wheel would aid a laboring craftsman greatly. Attached to a grinding or polishing tool, a lapidary could focus on refining a gem's facet without the need for a treadle.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: A largely unremarkable stone crucible, with metallic residue as evidence of its original use. The only notable detail is this embedded icon of Hermaeus Mora. Who could guess that the One Who Knows might enjoy jewelry?

2.name: Amalien
2.description: I've found shallow pans like this inside old Dwemer ruins, typically near areas where they built constructs. I assume they're related to the metalwork Dwarves were known for. Could this be evidence of Dwemer residing in Apocrypha?

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: Your fixations lead you astray, Amalien. The Dwarves likely used this for the same reason as armies do across Tamriel. For smelting alloys to repair armor. Perfect for quickly making a number of small rings or fasteners.

1.name: Gabrielle Benele
1.description: I've used little stoves like this in my office in Solitude. Quite effective in heating a room on a cold Skyrim evening. The vent on top is curious, and dangerous I must say. Perhaps its for making food?

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: One could produce food, though that's not the intended purpose. This stove can achieve very high levels of heat that would over-char your nightly leg of lamb. No, this device is meant for smelting metals. See how it attaches to a larger fixture?

3.name: Amalien
3.description: The decorative metal tendrils on the base caught my attention. I tested the stove's ability, and it does get unbearably hot. However, the tendrils stayed cold to the touch. I can't tell if its a quirk of the metal or Hermaeus Mora's influence.

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: A rod comprised of several wheels of various materials. I believe one is lead, perhaps another copper. Each wheel also has differing textures, some gritty while others more fine-grained. These remind me of sharpening stones.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: An excellent inference, Ugron, though these aren't for blades. Jewelry artisans use lapidary wheels like this for cutting and polishing gemstones. A row of them like this would be used by quite an expert.

3.name: Gabrielle Benele
3.description: Weapons, jewelry, what's really the difference? With the recent uptick in endowing jewels with magical properties, even a well-faceted diamond could cause physical harm.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: This may look like a simple rack for a work table, but these ornate tentacles tell another story. I believe that they conduct power from Hermaeus Mora into the tools hung here.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: Don't leap to conclusions about these decorations. Many cults adorn their tools with Mora's symbol. But for reverence, not power. The ancient Enraptured Order would drape octopuses across worktables as a sign of respect.

3.name: Gabrielle Benele
3.description: Amalien's intuition seems right this time, Reginus. These tentacle radiate a very slight Daedric power. Nothing dangerous, likely? But any tools hung on this rack would likely be imbued with some Apocryphal energies over time.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: Would be a nice piece of furniture if not for its immense weight. Wrought iron legs with stone shelving? My back hurts just thinking about lifting it into my study.

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: You should train with my clan, Reginus. They carry heavier furniture than this without any pain. Though, did you notice it belongs to a larger piece? I wonder if it was even meant to be moved.

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: Most certainly not. Examining these gnarled legs reveals they were once fused to a great slab of metal. What managed to separate these shelves from its larger structure is an open question, but I do not wish to meet something that strong.

1.name: Gabrielle Benele
1.description: For as old as these brass legs are, they appear in remarkable condition. The foot rests appear worn a bit, but I don't see the stress fractures that I expected. I wonder what accounts for their unusual strength?

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: We shouldn't discount simple high-quality craftsmanship. It's likely not even brass but some less common metal more suitable to sustaining heavy weight. These iron entanglements may help with support.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: The entanglements help more than you realize. They're not made of iron, but an unusual Daedric metal only found in Apocrypha. The strands infuse the brass legs providing significantly more strength. How rare to see something like this on Nirn!

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: A well-worn desktop made of a thick stone slab. I see etchings and gouges from tools, so likely this was once used as a work table. Somehow, it reminds me of the ancient stone coffins I've found.

2.name: Gabrielle Benele
2.description: I've seen similar stone coffins in my explorations, and I agree with the comparison. Not quite sure how to describe the sensation, but it feels dead. Have you noticed how cold it is to the touch?

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: You two have scared yourself into thinking this table is imbued with death when there's a simpler explanation. The table's stone absorbs heat, yes. An excellent quality for a jeweler working with hot metals.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: A simple for smaller items, even with clear Daedric decorations. Perhaps it channels power from Oblivion into whatever sits on the shelves. Perhaps a now-dispelled enchantment that contained cursed items?

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: An interesting supposition, though we'd have to test it for Daedric emanations. However, it does remind me of displays used by jewelers to show off their wares.

3.name: Gabrielle Benele
3.description: I performed all the tests I could for Daedric influence or curses in general. None of the results came back positive. Just a simple gem holder with an unsettling design. Or is it? It is.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: Beautiful decorative pieces. Jade stones set inside brass holders. The use of two stones side by side is unique and gives them the appearance of eyes. No doubt part of a larger design.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: Unsurprising that they look like eyes since Hermaeus Mora worshipers designed them. Decorative pieces like these appear on a number of furnishings and weaponry recovered from cultist bases. But are these more than decorative?

3.name: Gabrielle Benele
3.description: Good catch, Amalien. These pieces have a unique function. They seem to amplify and channel magicka that's directed at them. If arranged properly, they may funnel energy to a central point. An effective way to enchant jewelry, I'd guess.

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: Unusual material for shoe eyelets. Opalescent and energetically potent, I was surprised to see it holds a magicka charge in my standard intake tests. I'd bet Daedric in nature except I don't know of any Daedra that make pearls.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: Understandable miss on your part, my friend. The strange beasts of the Shivering Isles are rarely top of mind when we think of Oblivion. Check your references on the strange ecology the mad god has created in his Realm.

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: Well I'll be. I'd never heard of a Grummite or a Baliwog before! Let alone anything about this maddening maturation cycle. The cultist that sought out their pearls to use as materials was dedicated, talented, and I'd guess not all together sane.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: Testing indicates these thick laces were made from a Daedric fiber, crafted from the bark of the Gnarl. That places its origin as the Shivering Isles. Why or to what end this was done, I haven't a clue, but the business of cataloging carries on.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: It's been months since an item for catalog tried to kill me. Quite novel, this one, the laces crawled from their container and were trying to get up my nostrils when I woke and flung them across the room. Ugron talked me out of burning them.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: I've taken over this catalog so that Reginus doesn't burn yet another specimen. Tests have shown that the essence in these laces absolutely lives on. I'd wager that with hydration and nutrients a whole new Gnarl could be grown from just these fibers.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: Oddities abound, here. The sole of a shoe, that much is obvious, but the material is extremely strange. Absolutely not cowhide. And the top of the sole, pressing up against the bottom of the foot, has numerous Daedric glyphs burned into the hide.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: This has sparked my curiosity, Amalien. Tests show it is proofed against all manner of Oblivion realm materials. Made with hide from some Daedric beast, and shaped by cruel claws. This is why I focus on things like first Empire trade routes. Much simpler.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: We've had a run on artifacts from the Shivering Isles, so I took a leap. This is Grummite hide, a bipedal beast from Sheogorath's realm. Did one being shape the flesh of another? Or, disturbing thought, did a Grummite shape its own flesh into this sole?

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: This is ridiculous. I am a  serious researcher, damn it all. What Jester's Festival foppery is this toecap? This looks like the kind of thing Jester Queen Ayrenn would sell at a booth for the holiday.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: Ugron, you're lucky I went digging at your desk for your notes on that Akavari artifact. This isn't a holiday frippery, it's made with Amberweave Cloth and was stitched by a madness metal needle. This is from the Shivering Isles!

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: Putting this in the context of the Mad God's realm is a great discovery. Well done Amalien. My reading ties this toecap directly to Sheogorath himself, or perhaps a high level cultist. I'd bet it was used as part of a ceremonial outfit of some kind.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: An over-large heel made of thickly layered leather. I'm not sure what boot this would be appropriate for but the material here is resilient, almost magically so. My mind wanders to exotic materials, as it so often does. I will consult our samples.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: A Daedric creature called a Hunger donated its hide to the creation of this heel. My estimate is no less than three Hungers gave their hides to make this artifact. I've attempted to research anyone husbanding Hungers for materials and come up empty.

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: What a unique discovery! In collaboration with Amalein I've found reports of a "Hunger farm" somewhere in the Shivering Isles. The means, methods, and rationale behind establishing such a facility is something I will continue to pursue.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: This appears to be part of an articulated leather shoulder-piece. The double-moon design is a common Khajiit motif. The dagger-like emblem dividing the moons suggests the kingdom of Anequina, first century of the Second Era.

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: The design may appear common, but the material is highly unusual. It's terror-bird hide, which makes sense for the region. But it's been steeped in a strange oil or reagent, something dark and strong. I do not know it.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: Armor treated with techniques our Orc expert doesn't recognize? I think this arm cop was worn by a Khajiiti warrior who walked in dark places indeed. We're looking at something made for a dro-m'Athra, my friends!

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: A leather besagew, part of a larger piece of shoulder armor. Specifically, the besagew is a plate protecting the armpit. Don't be fooled by the bat-wing shape. It's made of layered terror-bird hide. Old Khajiit workmanship, but an unusual motif.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: I can explain the bat-wing design. In Elsweyr bats are sometimes associated with Namiira, their Great Darkness. Few Khajiit warriors would openly wear such a device unless they were devoted to the Bent Dance.

3.name: Gabrielle Benele
3.description: There is a word for Khajiit who give themselves to Namiira: dro-m'Athra. The dark coloration suggests the black fur of a cat lost to the Bent Dance, and the light-blue highlight represents the pale fire glowing in their soulless eyes.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: Small rivets such as these secure pieces of armor. They are fitted through slots so the plates can slide past each other; for example, as part of a shoulder piece. The rivets seem to be ebon steel, so this could be from a set of Dwemer armor.

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: You are mistaken. These rivets are made of moonstone ore, subsequently altered in a blacking process. Moonstone is the signature alloy of Khajiit metalcraft, but I have never seen it treated in this way. A very rare find indeed.

3.name: Gabrielle Benele
3.description: Altered moonstone would not only look different, its mystical properties would also be changed. Blackened moonstone would lend itself to enchantments of shadow and despair. I suspect the warrior who wore this was a champion of darkness.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: An old, well-made piece of leather armor intended to protect the top of the shoulder. The flourishes appear to be Khajiit in design, likely dating back to the late First Era. I feel there is something sinister about the design.

2.name: Gabrielle Benele
2.description: Sinister, indeed. The embellishments represent a void with something missing in the center--the Khajiit myth of Namiira and the heart of Lorkhaj. I believe this armor was worn by a powerful dro-m'Athra, a Khajiit who lost their soul to darkness.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: There are obscure Twilight Cantor songs that tell of a dro-m'Athra champion or warlord called the Fang of Lorkhaj. According to legend, there is only one Fang at a time. I think this armor belonged to one of those dark champions!

1.name: Amalien
1.description: This is rather mysterious! A black, heavy oil of some kind, preserved in a bronze vial of Khajiit craftsmanship. It rather looks like midnight in a bottle. I suppose it is some sort of alchemical admixture or reagent.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: Midnight in a bottle? Poetic nonsense. This is a glaze used to finish ceramics or metalwork. If you examine the vial, you can discern the image of an ancient Elsweyr warrior. I am surprised by the absence of a moon motif, though.

3.name: Gabrielle Benele
3.description: The moons are not absent, they are in eclipse. Khajiit born under the Dark Moon are susceptible to the Dark Heart, which ensnares them in the Bent Dance. I suspect the warrior on the vial is a Fang of Lorkhaj, a terrible dro-m'Athra champion.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: Lovely piece, exquisitely carved. Clearly it's the band of a ring. The engraving is hard to make out, but it seems Ayleid in origin. Perhaps Amalien's younger eyes will see something I can't.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: I'm always happy to oblige Reginus, and this finding is no different. The engraving is a small phrase of some sort. Something about balance and chaos? Could be part of a religious text, the material is well-worn.

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: It's a spell! A little-known reference in the unabridged Anuad tipped me off. This circular band acts as a foci for larger magical elements, though without those pieces I can't properly verify what the intended effect is.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Finely worked piece. Expert craftsmanship.  Ring bearing is smooth as a river stone, made of precious metal that must have been costly on its own. Masterwork of jewelry and design.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: I don't think this piece is as valuable as Muzah-Tei says it is. There's a strange imperfection in the center of the bearing. No gem or jewel would be able to sit correctly in it. This was an apprentice's first attempt at working with a new material.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Reginus doubts. Indentation similar to those found in First Era Saxhleel pieces. Allows for two stones or gems to nestle side-by-side. Well beyond a novice's skill. Duality was very important in early Anuic and Padomaic sects.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: I haven't seen a crest like this before. It's archaic, even by High Elf standards. The rigid, repetitive markings seem to suggest a sense of order or being part of a larger pattern. Perhaps it was worn as a boon or good luck token by the Ayleids?

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: It wouldn't have been worn alone. Look at the back, it's meant to be set into a larger piece. I recognize this marking, actually. It was printed on an ancient copy of the Anuad I once came across. The crest is Anu's, denoting protection and order.

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: Amalien's right. Surviving battle reports from the Ayleids suggest a two-fold stance warriors could take in battle. One defensive, the other offensive. The crest is a a signifier of those who prioritized defense and holding their ground in battle.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Excellent condition on sigil, serpent scales individually carved. Great care was taken here. Treasured homage to Sithis? More precious than the last unbroken egg in a clutch.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: Muzah-Tei speaks true, but his analysis leaves something to be desired. The sigil is incomplete, suggesting less the unbroken form of Sithis, and more the duality of Anu and Padomay. Could be Altmer in origin.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: Verita's comment got me thinking. Ayleid mythology describes a double-edged fighting form, harnessing order and chaos. This sigil is one half of a warrior's mark! Here, chaos represents recklessly striking down one's enemies on the battlefield.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: This bearing is so tiny and cute! But it still spins as smoothly as if it was fashioned yesterday. It almost reminds me of the cogs in Dwemer constructs, but it's made purely of stone. Can you imagine the expertise required for such a thing?

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: The quality suggests Elven origin, and the material is somewhat reactive to magicka. Could it be enchanted? Or have reacted to enchantments in a larger piece?

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: Jewelry isn't my strong suit, but this piece is interesting. Some ancient enchanted rings have mechanisms that allow the wearer to rotate a component, often for combat purposes. This gear would allow a mage to quickly adjust to combat mid-battle.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Delicate fret work. Well preserved despite sand and grit. Wind motif? No. Surging waters. Crashing waves. Perhaps a funerary plinth? Base for votives. Offerings. Unless we are looking at a stump missing its trunk.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: Take notice of the grooves along the plinth's edge and the less defined scratches near its center. I posit this was a merchant's plinth. A jewelry stand of some sort would account for the wear, with dangling necklaces leading to the scratches.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Why an additional stand when plinth works just as well? Defeats purpose of plinth. Although, must admit, grooves are sign of consistent wear. Repetitive motion. A stand for a tool or mechanism? Much to chew on.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: You should have seen my face when this piece of bismuth hit my desk. With the way it caught the moonlight, I thought I had found a piece of the Aurbis itself. Seems lighter than it should be, though. Can bismuth be hollow?

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: Have you tried coaxing the songbird from its nest? A swift hammer tap should suffice. Listen closely. Some birds sing at frequencies difficult for Altmer to hear.

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: I believe Muzah-Tei is asking if you have checked the bismuth for harmonic qualities. Surely you would have noticed drilled perforations had this bismuth been used for beadwork. Therefore, its hollow nature may be a sign of musical properties.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: I have come across an interesting piece of stonework, Verita. Fits comfortably in the palm of your hand and not of insignificant weight. I thought this may be a mercantile tool of some sort. Perhaps a weight to measure goods on a scale?

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: I could say the same about any stone found in a dig site. No, I believe this to be an embellishment. Note the small hole on the underside of the stone. Shallow, but purposeful. It may have decorated a tool or weapon.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: There seem to be signs of faded threads in the hole you noted, Verita. I've seen similar threading in Dwemer machinery, especially their finer mechanisms. Rather than an embellishment or weight, I believe this may be the head of a winding key.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: A gorgeous specimen to say the least. Clearly well-tended to, as no natural phenomenon would lead to such an even polish. A keepsake reminiscent of home? After all, culture can be found even in the odds and ends we carry with us.

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: Top of shell, yes, but interior as well. Circular grooves near edge twist towards mouth. Hermit crab, must be, but long lived. Remained with shell long enough to leave grooves. Fingerprints. This was a symbiotic relationship.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Of course. A treasured companion. I still remember brushing the coat of a mastiff I had as a child. The gentle work of this polish has taken on a new light, Muzah-Tei. Let us hope this crab merely outgrew its shell.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Discovered comb with delicate engravings. Kept in pocket and plucked idly. Strange result worth noting. Crabs everywhere. Coincidence? Laughter. Does a glyptodon sprout wings in the spring? Howling. I rest my scales.

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: There are battle hymns sung in Orsinium that tell of drumbeats that enraged local wildlife and could drive wolves towards your foes. Perhaps this comb offers a soothing melody to these crabs? Additionally, please explain your written laughter.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Clouds part, of course. A tide song held in these delicate metal teeth. Calming. Restorative. I must seek out its companion drum. Or, if none to be found, a Tide-Reader who may recognize its tune. Lastly, laughter offered so others may partake.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: An impressive specimen. I've seen similar skulls from Black Marsh, and it may be a related family. Rarely does one find one of this size and condition. A good varnish would help preserve it and keep the exposed bone from drying out too badly.

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: Reptiles such as this grow throughout their lives. This one might have seen the first arrivals of the High Elves to Solstice. I doubt it was happy about the situation. Even less so when it was defeated.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: It may have been more than just a simple trophy, though. I've seen notes that some Sithis sects revere these beasts as guardian animals. Perhaps it had help reaching this size, defending a temple all its long life.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: Bismuth is found in small quantities throughout Tamriel, but nowhere else do we see it in such abundances and size. The environment that allows such massive uniform accretion would be both impressive and unique.

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: Look at how it catches the light and refracts it within its structure. I wouldn't be surprised if it would have similar effects on other energies. But I sincerely doubt this structure was natural. Perhaps shaped by a culture that respected its natures?

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: A good catch Ugron. I believe this was shaped by a Stone-Nest Argonian tribe, this is almost identical to ancient markers that indicated a xanmeer building site. I've never seen one made with such a novel material though!

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: I've seen smaller versions of these totems in Black Marsh, dating back to pre-Duskfall times. Precisely dating them could indicate when the Stone-Nest people first arrived on Solstice.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: I have a theory that early waves of settlers on Solstice, aided by supernatural forces, crafted such large blocks and moved them into position through levitation spells.

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: Stone carvings in such patterns are common among the Argonians, and there is no question of local variance and creativity. They're often used as markers for sacred sites, or waystones to guide travel. One might assume this was used in a similar fashion, but who can say?

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: A massive crocodile ribcage! Most of one, anyway. It's quite an impressive curiosity, but I doubt that it's anything more than a trophy taken long ago by some well-off hunter in Black Marsh.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: This no hunter's trophy. Look at the carvings on the bones, Argonian. The people of Black Marsh are known to preserve legendary beasts who have acted as temple guardians.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Argonian yes. Black Marsh, no. Sithis-worshipping Argonians on the isle of Solstice husband these enormous beasts as temple guardians. This is likely a remnant of a stalwart defender of a secret, sacred site.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: Alas, this appears to be one of those occasions where old trash is mistaken for historic treasure. Skeletal crocodile tails such as this were popular in Leyawiin in the 3rd century of the Second Era. You could buy one from any street merchant.

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: Look at the size of this thing. Surely no street vendor carried this. And, I believe this came from no crocodile in Black Marsh. The fine scale pattern near the tip? That is found in a crocodile breed from the island of Solstice. And I promise you Solstice Argonians were not selling them as souvenirs.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Then this is the rare occasion where something historic is mistaken for old trash! I have found stories, perhaps just tall tales, but they say that these crocodiles were once so massive multiple Argonian riders rode into battle against Daedric invaders. Perhaps this is a remnant from that singular age.

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: A household totem, rather common in Black Marsh. Argonians consider lizards to be clever and lucky. This totem is old and quite well made. I suspect it belonged to a shaman or chief of some importance.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: Lizard? Actually, this is a representation of an iguana. Which is a lizard, of course, but one found primarily on the island of Solstice. I doubt very much that this totem comes from Black Marsh.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Indeed. The Stone-Nest Saxhleel of Solstice admire iguanas for their fearlessness and tenacity. The carving technique marks it as eastern Solstice. 28th century of the First Era. Hardly a common totem at all.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: Here we have a soapstone figurine, carved in the shape of a massive Argonian. Clearly, the figure depicts an Argonian behemoth--a tribal totem, perhaps. It could be centuries old; it's hard to tell with soapstone.

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: Argonian behemoths are fearsome warriors. See the faint scoring marks? Soapstone is soft, but even so it takes a long time for etched lines to wear smooth. The style is strange, too. Mid-First Era, but from where?

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: I am not surprised the style is strange to you. This totem comes from the Stone-Nest saxhleel of Solstice. 11th or 12th century. It depicts a vahath behemoth, a warrior cursed to relish excessive violence and death.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: This enormous totem is carved in the shape of an distended skull? I think this marked a forbidden place. I suspect it dates back to the Blackwater War. Resisting Argonians often warned the invading Imperials to stay away from their holy places.

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: Saxhleel totems can stand for many things. A skull almost always stands for Raj-Sithis, destroyer and bringer of change. However, I have never seen a Black Marsh Nisswo carry or display a totem quite like this.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: I can shed some light on that! Corelanya accounts of their early years in exile on Solstice mention a secret cult of Argonian assassins known as "Death Dancers." The Elven records describe similar totems left by the bodies of their victims. So this is likely a death cult icon from that distant isle.

1.name: Amalein
1.description: Notes with this catalog say it was apparently found while following a cute, three-toed creature. Beautiful. I wonder about the significance of the conch shells. Just a plentiful material for the artisan?

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: These carvings look Argonian, I believe from the remote Tide-Born group on the distant isle of Solstice. From what little I know of them, this piece may serve as a symbolic connection to the sea.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: You have it right. The conch whispers from deep waters. As a people they are never far from the waters that gave them life. With this they carry the song of the tides with them.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: This item for catalog comes to us from the distant isle of Solstice. Made, perhaps, to collect fresh rainwater? But the choice of materials and the worked wave markings suggest ceremonial importance of some kind.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: Notes attached to the find indicates it was buried in the sand along a beach. Why would one need to bring fresh water to the ocean? What a curious ritual.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: The warmth of the tides sits well upon the scales. But salt is terrible for the eyes. Celebrants plunge their face within the basin and gaze deep, seeing what the tides seek to show them without the sting.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: I've seen celebrants carry similar crests after undergoing their chukka-sei ritual of change. But none like this. At first glance, a reward? But why wear a prized crest into battle? Maybe charms from loved ones? Rituals may have gotten more intense after invasive arrivals on Solstice. The Tide-Born had to grow. They needed to change.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: An ancient map of Solstice. Ancient Argonian settlements dot the map like the spots of an ancestor lizard. There were so many more villages then. Tide-Born on the coast and Stone-Nest further inland.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: Yes, the Corelanya Elves certainly changed the face of Solstice. Their colonization of the island likely contributed to the loss of the smaller Argonian settlements. Sunport was barely worth noting on this map.

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: One must wonder what the next iteration of a Solstice map will contain. The scar of the Writhing Wall will be worth including, most likely. But what else will change before the next cartographer puts pen to paper?

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: A simple stone for a complex task. To connect a family through the ages. Stone is chipped to have many small indentations. Stone-Nest tradition says each face retains some flavor, some memory, of meals past.

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: Stones are passed down through generations. A  soup stone in a new home's cookpot may represent centuries of meals. The stone remembers, it is said, and passes the wisdom of past cooks to the family around the table.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: These soup stones demonstrate the importance of family and community among my distant Stone-Nest kin. When one partakes of a meal, one joins the history of the family serving it. And so contributes to its future.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: Chisels! Hand picks! Stone-headed mallets! The Stone-Nest Argonians created towering wonders from such beautifully simple tools. Their xanmeers remain intact even after centuries of exposure. It makes me think they may be enchanted somehow.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: Stone-Nest artistry remains a wonder, but not a magical one. I've had a thaumaturgical associate examine these tools and they are no more magical than I am. A testament to their ingenuity, dating back centuries.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Indeed, their tools are as durable as their monuments. I believe at least ten generations of scaled hands have used these items. To think, these may have helped shape a xanmeer's stone coffin not long after the Argonians arrived on Solstice!

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: From artisan's apogee to a misshapen lump. Examining the undamaged elements makes me think this may have originally been sculpted by Skivoxo, a Dremora artisan from the First Era. But look at the damage! The sigil is shattered, the eye-gems are pried out, and I believe it was used as a well-weight at one point. Now as much a commentary on the God of Schemes as an art piece.

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: A leather cowl of Reachfolk workmanship. Reach shamans still wear such coverings as part of various beast-themed headdresses or warmasks, but I suspect this is quite old. I do not recognize the leather.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: That's because this is no ordinary leather. It's made of hide blessed for shape-changing. I imagine it belonged to a powerful Reachfolk shaman, a follower of Hircine. He is the Father of Manbeasts, after all.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Uraccanach the Witchman described the Manbeast as one of the five aspects of Hircine that Reachfolk worship. They call this aspect Storihbeg. He comes to the wild places of Nirn to hunt with his children, the Skinshifters.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: Is this a scarf? No, it's a headwrap made from some sort of felt. I believe it is part of a ceremonial Reachfolk mask. A shaman or chief would wear this beneath the mask itself. Curious. The cloth part of a mask is usually the first part to rot away.

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: It is not felt made from wool, but the fur of a fox. A Reachfolk mask incorporating fox-fur certainly suggests Hircine worship. A fox is one of the Huntsman's aspects.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Reachfolk know that aspect of Hircine as Gulibeg, the Quick Fox. He seeks to confound mortal hunters and run them in circles until they are so confused they follow him over a cliff or into a mire.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: Now this is interesting. A carved wooden face-mask in the shape of a snarling beast's snout. I saw similar relics when I visited the Shrine of the Hunt-Father in Markarth. The shaman there explained that it represented an aspect of Hircine.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: That's Hrokkibeg, the Mighty Bear. Reachfolk believe he comes to our world seeking solitude and a renewal of his spirit, but beware. If you disturb his rest, he will tear you asunder!

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: Ancient Nedic heroes of the Ket Keptu often wore bear emblems or totems. I think the war-mask this snout was a part of must have belonged to an important war-chief or hunt-leader. A champion of Hircine.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Hmm. A flask of oil, such as that used by woodworkers or leatherworkers to finish their handiwork. But I do not recognize the odor, nor the stag device inscribed on the flask. All I can say is that it is very old.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: I know the stag symbol. It is fairly commonplace in the Reach. It represents one of the aspects of Hircine, the Great Stag. This oil is sacred to Hircine, likely used to anoint and consecrate a relic of great value.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: Oh! That would be Uricanbeg. Those who hear the drumbeat of his hooves are doomed to run with the herd. To be chased and unmade, as the Reachfolk say. A warrior wearing the mask imbued by this oil would drive his enemies from him in terror.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: Teeth? No, fangs. The scrimshaw is definitely Reachfolk work. I believe the markings represent a chant to Hircine in his aspect as Alrabeg, the Hunter: The five are all, the five are one. Five are true and death-in-the-woods.

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: Five is a number that comes up a lot with Hircine. These fangs represent the Spear of Bitter Mercy, also called Spear with Five Points. They would have been fixed in a warmask belonging to a great chief of the Ket Keptu.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Ah, of course! The Ket Keptu were hunters and warrior-smiths, a people devoted to the Lord of the Hunt. To carry the Spear of Bitter Mercy was a high honor for their great champions. Whoever wore this warmask was indeed favored by Hircine!

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: A simple, but effective, mechanism for pulling a wagon. Given the style and color of the wheel's material, it's indicative of early Worm Cult designs, likely originating in the early second era.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: But look at the carvings! The wheel doesn't just rotate, it has these accent elements that give the appearance of a writhing worm with in every turn of the wheel. A nod to the cult's patron, Molag Bal. Perhaps a means to frighten enemies!

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: The reinforcement of the wheel itself is what intrigues me. It's unnecessary for an ordinary cargo wagon. It was likely attached to some battle equipment or heavy supplies. I've seen portable forges with wheels like this in Orsinium.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Impressive specimen, as troughs go. Tempered by fire. Carved like a canyon. Used in blacksmithing to cool the metal to an acceptable temperature and rigidity. Ancient and well-used. The tool of a master.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: Note the rather sinister carvings that adorn this trough. Not unlike the forge tools of modern-day Worm Cultists, though more ornate. And meant to  slot in alongside another element of some kind. Look here, fire discoloration. Perhaps an ember box?

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: Most certainly a Worm Cultist's tool. The size, however, is interesting. It's smaller than similar troughs from the same era, implying a level of portability. The cult always has need of weapons and tools, I suppose. Why not forge them on the move?

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Rare to see an anvil this small, like a fleshfly in a marsh. Unimpressive, on its own. But traveling smiths and artisans can make great use of even a tiny anvil like this one. The skill of the crafter is what matters.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: I recognized the Daedric motifs on this anvil immediately! The design clearly indicates an allegiance to Molag Bal, perhaps invoking his protection on the crafter. And this metal! I'd wager this comes from forge-wells of Coldharbour. Fascinating!

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: Got practical with this one and regretted it immediately. Struck a hammer to the anvil and was thrown across my office. The infernal thing is enchanted. Runes prevent casual investigation, perhaps a more practiced adventurer will get some use out of it.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: Exquisite example of early Second-Era Worm Cult craftsmanship. Given the size and placement of the hook, it was likely attached to a wagon or cart in a larger convoy. It may have been used to signal movements or orders to cohorts in the group.

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: Not just a lantern, a necromantic one at that. It's made of bone, but not anything that grew naturally in this shape. The cult is known for their proficiency in the ossiform arts. The lantern shape was coaxed from pre-existing remains.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Out of academic curiosity, I lit the lantern. The flame it produces is haunting. I wager it was used to light a forge or ritual enchantment. I didn't place anything in the fire itself, but it was surprisingly warm, given the strange color of the flame.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: Looks to me to be the bed of a wagon. Relatively simple, all things considered, though it is ancient. Sturdy wood, slightly charred in some places. Perhaps it was taken into battle?

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: This piece has seen some action - just not battle. The scorch marks are more indicative of forgework. The sturdy wood and some lingering enchantments suggest someone knew this wagon would be in close proximity to flame.

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: Evidence of portable forges has been found as early as the First Era. The ability to craft and use weapons or tools on the move is crucial to commerce and battle. This was a blacksmithing cart, belonging to the Worm Cult if the carvings are correct.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: At first glance, I thought this might be a soul gem. But holding it felt so strange! The crystal almost pulses like a beating heart on fire! And yet it feels so empty. Soul Gems have a different warmth.

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: Crystal has the essence of a soul, but not its cry. Glows like a torchbug in a lantern. Fragile like a new egg. Develops cracks at the slightest handling.

3.name: Ugron-Gro-Thumog
3.description: I have reports here of Worm Cultists carrying these after the Writhing Wall erupted on Solstice. They carry specks of souls only meant to be crushed for power. I suggest we hide away this vile tool.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: I've been assured by allies in the Mages Guild this gate's connection to Coldharbour has been permanently severed. So it's something of a bizarre art piece now, nothing more or less. Amalien, I imagine you might enjoy this?

2.name: Amalien
2.description: You know I do! With help I've been able to review usage of this gate since it's construction. It was instrumental in moving forces from Coldharbour through to Nirn for their campaign on Solstice. A portal for war.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: Further investigation with a Knight of the Lamp has revealed the soul-being of Prince Naemon was escorted to Nirn via this gate. Fascinating. I'll send inquiries to the Fellowship, I wonder if the Queen knows about this.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: A single pendulum in the easily recognizable style of the Stone-Nest Argonians of Solstice. No doubt intended to act as a trap to defend one of their sacred xanmeer. But what if it could be set to swinging? Perhaps a metronome on a massive scale?

2.name: Amalien
2.description: This might even be popular among the hatchlings! The pendulum ball seems just the right size for a little one to sit and swing on. More likely, as with the massive clockworks of Sotha Sil's realm, some were used to mark the passage of the years.

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: I'm given to understand even to this day traders will pay a fair price for an intact xanmeer pendulum. Calendar-keeping, traps, oracular divining, these things offer a number of potential uses. And beautifully crafted, if such a thing stirs you.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: Exquisite architecture, but a shame to see such extensive damage. Some materials research indicates this was done by coldfire blasts. Necromancy of some kind.

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: Hard to tell age with Stone-Nest structures. Built to last. Though elders say time is a tide that smooths all stones. Most likely, damaged in the fight with Clan Corelanya. But this could be far, far older.

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: Agreed. And consistent with reports I've read of Clan Corelanya tactics on the battlefield. Some of their greatest bone colossi struck with the weight of an anvil and a terrible blue soul fire. As Verita said. A shame.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: This pillar screams Stone-Nest to me. Beautiful and fearsome in equal measure! If it was a quarter of the size I'd stick it under Verita's bed at night to shock him in the morning.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: I have seen more fearsome things than this beneath my bed, Amalien. While largely ornamental, I believe these pillars also served a symbolic cultural or religious purpose. Perhaps they acted as xanmeer wardens, vouchsafing these temples from danger.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: I'd never approve of such a thing, Amalien. Just for the record. Artifacts like this can be found in every culture on the continent, dripping with symbolic significance. Few are quite as expertly made, though. Stunning.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: Fascinating! A furnace from Oblivion, Coldharbour most likely. I'm reminded of works by Klasius Malik, a scholar specializing in exactly this kind of artifact. I'll do some reading to refresh my memory on the subject.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: Scholar Malik has proven to be a most engaging author! Coldharbour's blue flames are unique to that realm, fueled as they are by the souls taken by the Prince and the cult. I expected the flame to eventually dissipate, but it still burns strong even now.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: In further writings Malik specifically notes that the blue flames are also used to power Coldharbour's arcane engines. Perhaps this was once part of a larger apparatus? Let's hope it stays quiet here on Nirn.

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: I'd like to suggest a direction for our study: why only the head? Was this simply a mantlepiece sculpted by a Molag Bal follower, or was it severed from a larger statue?

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: I and Ugron examined the head, and we've both determined this head was severed from a larger piece. Devotedly built and dispassionately destroyed. A clean cut, as if from an artisan's knife.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Skivoxo the Dread Sculptor, a Dremora artisan from Coldharbour. I'd recognize the work anywhere. Perhaps the artist himself severed the head? His current whereabouts are unknown. Perhaps he and his Daedric patron had some kind of falling out?

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: A repulsive design. Something only a cultist could love. Notes from the field indicate arcane engines derived from this design were capable of the darkest of magic. A note of caution to my fellow scholars.

2.name: Ugron-gro Thumog
2.description: I might be wrong, but I'm seeing some similarities with some elements of this design and touchstones in Stone-Nest xanmeer designs? I can't imagine the Argonians of Solstice creating a weapon of fear like this, though.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Consulted with Stone-Nest elders. Heard dark tales, ancient lore. Stolen designs fuel hateful magics. Shut this away friends. Let us not speak of it again.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: An excellent example of Stone-Nest Argonian ingenuity. The device at its heart is a simple machine, a stone block balanced to allow easy movement at a touch. Cunningly simple, but can open enormous doors or operate deadly traps.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: Counter weight mechanics like this could operate titanic doors, mobile platforms, and walking statues. All carved from living stone. A testimony to the inventiveness of the Stone-Nest Argonians. They had the skill and artisanship to craft these devices while much of mainland Tamriel was still living in straw huts.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: As a device, very useful. But we cannot ignore the fine craftsmanship as well. Stone-Nest artisans believe a thing like this is more than simply a mass of pulleys, weights, and rope. It is art in and of itself.

1.name: Regina Buca
1.description: A challenge to identify any statue from a single limb. But the carving here, in particular the tight musculature and claws, identifies it as part of a statue of Molag Bal. Prince of Domination. The Dremora sculptor Skivoxo, if I'm any judge of Oblivion artisans.

2.name: Urgon gro-Thumog
2.description: Itâs interesting to see a statue fragment of Molag Bal this large. Usually one either encounters a full statue maintained by devoted followers or scattered fragments smashed to smithereens. Perhaps there was something special about this statue?

3.name: Amalien
3.description: What fine craftsmanship! The tension in the muscles indicates a fine understanding of anatomy, and the blood vessels almost seem to pulse with life! Then again, knowing it was made by a Dremora I'm sure that understanding came from all kinds of unpleasant activities and now I've gone and made myself ill.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: At first glance, a simple ring mold made from an uncommon material. It is porous and lightweight, yet rigid. Pumice stone? The mold itself offers no insight into the ring it once gave shape. Its band and face are without detail. Perhaps a signet?

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: Not pumice. Bone. Compact exterior with a webbed, sponge-like interior. Gives the mold its rigidity. Very uncommon material for jewelry, that much is certain. First I have ever seen. Impossible to say what creature this came from. Most curious.

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: Impossible? I'm surprised, Muzah-Tei. The bone belongs to a Bearer of Fargrave. The webbed structure of their bones shimmer when placed under starlight. In the future, send bones to me. It will save us all some time.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: Not to alarm anyone, but whenever I peer into the gem's fractured facets, I see my face not only as it is, but countless variations. Old and young, pallid and bright-eyed. I don't know what to make of it. It's unnerving.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: I imagine the pallid and haggard reflections are the most presently accurate? I suggest taking a break from your work. Enjoy the feeling of grass between your quill bruised fingers. I am certain what you're seeing is, at best, an illusory trick.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: We have already ruled out illusions. And by we I mean my variances. Lovely group once we got past the stunned silence. Is that conceited of me if they are each, seemingly, me? Regardless, we're working diligently to solve this mystery, worry not!

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Discovery reminds me of similar finds found sifting through the sands of Fargrave. Does not strike me as mundane jewelry material. There is a hum to it. A warmth. A powerful compulsion to keep it for myself. As such. Take precautions.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: A beautiful sample indeed, Muzah-Tei. I believe this is Aetheric Gold. A rare material imbued, so the story goes, with the light of the Aetherius. Not that such a thing can be measured. A parlor trick to increase its price, I'm certain of it.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Perhaps, Verita, the beauty of this discovery is dulled by your mercantile horse blinders. What I see here fills my mind with the ringing of Zenithar's anvil. Faith made tangible, perhaps. You merely have to know what to look for.

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: These ensorcelled strategies confound me. These are not the first bewitched battle plans I have studied, but the solution to their obfuscation has proven to be the most illusive. At least I am certain one of you will enjoy this puzzle.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: I've asked my assistant to bring me every lens available to us to try and find some combination that parts this shimmering mess. Apologies for the curtness. This puzzle, as you call it, is giving me a headache.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: You lot are always good for a laugh. These aren't battle plans, they're charcoal rubbings. And they aren't under an enchantment. Rather, I believe this rubbing has captured all possible variations of its subject. Remarkable.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: When I first discovered this vial, I thought for certain its brilliance was a result of its crystal container, but the light shines from the oil itself. I've grown to enjoy its soft, refracted light across the walls of my study.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: What a brilliant find. Only once before have I come across such an oil. It was sold by a merchant who frequents the bazaars of Fargrave. I believe he called it Starlight Oil? A distillation of light from Fargrave's night skies.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: Starlight Oil? Of course! Distilled light can be made from any natural light source, but the most potent is starlight. It requires an arduous exposure process over decades and, as such, is reserved for only the most precious of enchantments.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: Grand. Daedra-Crushing. And if that doesn't give away the Imperial make, the armor does. Built just after Leovic's time, which makes sense. May have been an artistic refutation of the dead Emperor.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: I may be seeing things, but does it look like to anyone else that there might be markings behind the helm? Particularly at the base of the neck? My eyes might be playing tricks, though. I was up late last night studying a strange liquid, in detail.

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: Daedric runes on an Imperial statue! Etched under the helm, amazing catch Amalien. I had to squint even with my magnifying glass. They translate to something like "Nirn shall burn." Whoever built this statue must have been a follower of the dead emperor.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: A Fargrave Bearer's skull, here in our galleries! You should have seen the size of the portal, this is absolutely enormous! We owe a great contribution to the adventurer that sent this along. You all must see this with your own eyes.

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: Some say the Fargrave Bearers were Daedra. Others say they were beyond comprehension, mortal or Daedric. Regardless, I've seen my share of skulls in burial chambers and battlefields. We're all the same underneath. Only our stories set us apart.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Well said. In the end, we all return to Aetherius, our bones a remnant. And these bones. Strange story and even stranger origins. Beings whose very purpose is lost to time, forgotten ash. Eternally grateful to witness them firsthand.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: Apparently the Valenwood tradition of skulls as percussive instrumentation dates back to at least the First Era. Though, a friend of mine in the Vinedusk Rangers tells me they're still made and used to this day.

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: These instruments are a beautiful, if grim, reminder of the Wood Elf relationship with death and the Green. Also, your friend wouldn't happen to be Glooredel, would it? Tell her the desk in my office still has a blistered acid stain thanks to her.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: I'm going to ask someone at the Mages Guild to examine these enchantments, very different than their modern counterparts. So simple, yet so powerful. Fascinating! Also, yes, it was Gloo. And I have a fire salt burn scar on my ankle to prove it.

1.name: Amalien
1.description: A massive mandibular remnant of Fargrave and Mirrormoor. A good opportunity to study their teeth! The teeth of a predator, as most Daedra tend to be. Hmm, there might the cornerstone of a thesis on Oblivion-realm dentition in this antiquity.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: You bring up an interesting notion, Amelien. We know so little about extra-Nirn ecosystems. The question of if Daedra truly need to eat to survive is one I continue enjoy debating with Ugron.

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: At next lunch, Verita. I believe the teeth speak to their role as defenders. Remember, the legends state these beings "held up the Celestial Palanquin" on their shoulders, moving the realm from place to place. Helps them look fearsome.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: The minute detail of curling toes. Sharp nails, despite the passage of time. A great cat, a dragon. Ambiguous, most likely intentional. The Khajiit of the distant past certainly took pleasure in their whimsy.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: Well said. Akatosh, the dragon god of time. Alkosh, to the Khajiit. This dragon, cat, time symbolism is common across a number of artifacts I've studied from the southern part of the continent, but the scale of this artifact is stunning. Why make an hourglass this large?

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Metal whispers of a place beyond Nirn. Could the study of their cat dragon god have led some to venture beyond the savannah, to Aetherius itself? When one is tracking a beast, after all, one must follow where its footprints lead.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: A lovely bulletin board, clearly handcrafted but well-used. It appears to be Covenant in style, perhaps originating in Daggerfall? I wonder what notices would have been pinned here. Seems the owner had a propensity for planning.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: Verita passed this one along to me. I found scraps of paper tucked along the trim. It's honestly baffling. There are portraits of what appear to be nobles and merchants, a map of the city, and various ledgers. What's the connection between them?

3.name: Amalien
3.description: I simply adore intrigue! There's only one answer: a plan for a heist! The portraits are the marks, the old map of Daggerfall has blind alleys and deadends marked for the getaway, and the ledger denotes the value of the stolen goods. Just thrilling!

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Good, hardy material. Most likely from the forests of Glenumbra. Crafted with care, but feels hollow. Could be hiding more secrets inside. One must listen carefully to the wood.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: What a fascinating design! The cabinet clearly has some sort of secret drawer or compartment, but I can't seem to find a keyhole for it. Maybe an enterprising mage sealed it with a spell?

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: Amalien is correct. There are secret compartments within this cabinet. But she will find that cleverly concealed pressure points and disguised buttons are much more convenient to the common thief than a complicated spell.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: As long as there have been possessions, there have been those who want to steal them. The symbol on the box looks like a primitive version of the Thieves Guild insignia. The tools are unfamiliar to me, but presumably used for some kind of theft.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: Reginus is right. These are certainly the tools of a thief. The long-handled devices remind me of typical lockpicks, though somewhat blunter in design than modern tools. I confess I've had little occasion to handle such contraband myself.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: The tools of a thief, yes. But not for any door. Just for one. A special set, carved to open one lock in particular. What treasure was worth such an effort?

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Well-worn leather, dyed dark as the night. Hood is big enough to cover the head, but wide enough to preserve lines of sight. Sewn to hide the wearer, like a whisper on the wind.

2.name: Ugron-gro Thumog
2.description: A thief's hood, most certainly. The lightweight leather provides protection from projectiles without weighing down the wearer or clunking around like a large helm. That said, the best thieves are the ones who don't get caught in the first place.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: I'm not sure if this hood is lucky or not. It's been patched in multiple places, and there are some concerning rust-colored stains. It saw plenty of action. But did its previous owner retire or find themselves on the wrong side of a guard's blade?

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: A short, brutal blade. The handle is reminiscent of traditional Daggerfall metalsmithing, though the blacksmith's mark has been scratched out. Someone wanted this dagger to be untraceable.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: Perhaps the blade was stolen from its owner? You can use smithing marks to trace the origin of a blade, which some owners take pride in. But it's not a very finely crafted dagger, so why would someone want to obscure its provenance?

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: This isn't the weapon of some noble or merchant. It's a short, wickedly sharp blade. The type of thing you press against some poor soul's throat while robbing them blind. The owner was a brigand who likely wanted to avoid detection.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: Hmm. This is obviously a devotional bas-relief commemorating the Divine Zenithar, and in remarkably good condition as well! It must have been protected from the elements soon after its creation.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: Definitely Zenithar - you can tell by the anvil. Rumors say that one similar to this hung in a merchant hall in a large city, but was removed surreptitiously by a rival guild in the dead of night, hidden, and never recovered.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: Yes. Zenithar, the Divine of Industry and Commerce. A worthy Divine. This is a fine piece, probably carved from the living stone by devoted Resolutes, probably in High Rock. It may have hung in the armory of a Fighters Guild once.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: The symbols of three Divines are shown here. Zenithar, the god of commerce. Stendarr, the god of mercy. And Akatosh , the Dragon god of time. They should be read bottom to top, with Akatosh as the foundation and the most important.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: Looking at the iconography, I would say the work is Breton in origin. Their pantheon venerates all three Divines. This may have hung in the shrine or cloister of a small mansion to honor several deities at once, thereby covering all bets.

3.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
3.description: Typical Breton religious handiwork. Three gods crowding one panel. They have too many of them, you know. Mind you, my people recognize this lot as divine beings, but Mauloch is the only one worth worshiping.

1.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
1.description: I can imagine the looks on the faces of anyone coming across this cache! It's counterfeit, of course, but the sheer amount of it would make a Dragon catch its breath in greed.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: The coins themselves are iron pyrite, a shiny but otherwise innocuous mineral. You can tell by the fact it wafts a small hint of sulfur. The gems are glass. In total, it is an amusing deception.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: The others fail to realize the amount of work put into creating such a fraudulent display. An aura of effort surrounds it like flames, hiding its workmanship beneath a veneer of gold.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: A most disturbing display. See how Hircine looms above the scene, commanding his minions beneath a full moon? You can feel the raw vitality and energy of the tapestry in every cord of it. A worthy acquisition.

2.name: Muzah-Tei
2.description: Look at the warp and weft. Look at the tensile durability of the fabric. The subject it describes matters not! This is a precious creation, lovingly crafted by expert, civilized hands. Brilliant.

3.name: Amalien
3.description: Its artistry is unquestionable. Its subject matter is troubling. Perhaps this once hung on the walls of a werewolf lord, or was laid before the hearth of a worshiper of the Daedric Prince Hircine.

1.name: Tuindoril
1.description: Simply the most stunning example of Dwemeric design I have yet to encounter, and I have absolutely no idea what it does. With most artifacts pulled from a construct, context clues and structural elements allow for an educated guess. Not so, here.

2.name: Tuindoril
2.description: Every analysis I have thrown at this thing just confirms how inscrutable it is. I believe it to be a device used for tracking the status of a system or phenomenon. But what system, or what phenomenon, it observes is well beyond me.

3.name: Tuindoril
3.description: Nothing else for it, Iâve taken my initial notes and written an entire thesis on this device. My advice, for the researchers that will follow in my footsteps, is to assume nothing. Seek answers in the subsurface Aetherius. Be bold.

1.name: Reginus Buca
1.description: A simply exquisite centerpiece, to be sure, but deeply interesting on a cultural level. Any time you see imagery like this you think Maormer, perhaps Thras. But all of the design work I see here hints at old Bretonic, perhaps even Direnni craftsmanship.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: This fountain captures the beauty of nature and uses a number of natural materials. But nothing about this is natural. Itâs fakery mimicking nature. A neat little encapsulation of the cultural transition from the Direnni Hegemony to Bretonic rule.

3.name: Reginus Buca
3.description: I believe these flowing waters represent the beautiful Abecean and its role in daily life across High Rock. The role of this endless tide in proto-Breton culture, its function in conveying the Elves to the region. All as a mudcrab ballet.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: A beautiful example of recent artistry mimicking the beauty of the past. A miniature Ra Gada sailing vessel. Meticulously crafted, with its sails frozen mid-billow on a hand-carved sea. A moving testament to the artistâs lineage.

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: I know this is an art piece. But if this is based on passed-down knowledge there are some fascinating details to be gleaned about Yokudan ship construction. Iâve a friend in Gonfalon Bay who lives for this. Iâll have to get her a schematic.

3.name: Verita Numida
3.description: After careful observation I believe some of the materials here may be from the Yokudan diaspora! Some elements of the ship, stone from the base. A testament to a family who didn't abandon their home, but carried it with them.

1.name: Tuindoril
1.description: A bell out of legend! With provenance provided by a spectral seafarer. Baron-Captain Olsien Guy Mard received this bell, enchanted by the archmage Syrabane, in exchange for his pledge of the Riotous Redress to the All-Flags Navy.

2.name: Tuindoril
2.description: My initial repairs to this enchanted object were done out of necessity. I now curse my eager hands. Even a small error could have undone a magical lattice Iâd challenge any other mage of this era to duplicate. Let alone understand.

3.name: Tuindoril
3.description: I stand corrected. Iâm looking at twenty pages of notes from one Telenger the Artificer, who has much to say on this beautiful artifact. Suffice it to say, itâs powerful. Unique. And vaguely shocking it was entrusted to a pirate like Guy Mard.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Frozen in stone since Tamrielâs distant past, Merethic minerals have transformed this creature. No end to opportunities for study, but strange to see the illusion of this ancient beast scuttling across a long-forgotten shore.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: As usual my friend, your understated observations are a joy to page through. Natural history is such a fascinating subject. Who would have imagined the humble mudcrab was alive even in the day so the ancients?

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Further study reveals interesting wrinkle. Fine details are similar to those of immature mudcrabs today. Despite its size, full grown to my eye, this beast is just a baby. If thatâs so, how large were mudcrabs of Merethic era?

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Perfectly preserved. Sturdy body. So like the hoppers of today, but with hints at a world so unlike our own. Observe thickness of spines on the back. What ate this?

2.name: Ugron gro-Thumog
2.description: The details are fascinating. Under close observation you can make out scales, gills, and the nuances of the fins. And what the rock itself implies is just as interesting. Hewâs Bane is far from the current bounds of Black Marsh, after all.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Careful use of tinctures shows hints of pigment. Brilliant turquoise, amber, and crimson. True to life from that bygone era? A reminder that even ancient beasts can tell stories that have survived endless empires.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Under arcane lights, shimmering bands of black and silver stone. Preserves every detail of a predator's fearsome anatomy. Large, dominating, and born to hunt ancient rivers. Imagine a swarm rising around you.

2.name: Verita Numida
2.description: Itâs worth noting, my dear colleague, that predators and scavengers like this have morphology matching their diet. And so look at the size of these teeth! Imagine the size of the beasts they consumed crossing these ancient rivers of yours.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Sampled stone, much analysis. Deep rivers, thorny marshes. Like the southern tip of the continent but so unlike our world of today. These slices of the past tell us so much but open so many questions at the same time. Dries my scales.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Yaghra from an ancient seabed. Physically similar, but look close. Plates of armor softer. Details of arms subtly different. A distant cousin to those of today? A variant made by the sorcerers of Thras? Where do you come from?

2.name: Amalien
2.description: Iâve been staring at this thingâs head and I wonder if it was less adapted to the surface? In the ancient past were these beasts restricted to the depths? And why does it seem still ready to strike, millennia later?

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: These creatures are no doubt tied to the history of Thras, but how? Were Yaghra created by the Sload? Transformed from another creature entirely? This fossil hints they have been around for eons. Maddening to only see on page in this tale.

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: Used arcane lights for further study. Storm in stone speaks to minerals where it died. Does not sing of deep ocean. Trees, flowers, petals. A massive fish in a shallow sea.

2.name: Amalien
2.description: Tamriel of today has nothing like it, but Iâve read stories from ancient kingdoms where the seas ranged far and wide and teemed with noisome life. Another reminder of Apocrypha.

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: Clues adding up. Natural life, touched by the tentacles of a Daedric Prince? How much of Tamrielâs past was shaped by natural process. And how much was influenced by the whims of Oblivion?

1.name: Muzah-Tei
1.description: A tremendous specimen. Under the arcane lights of the Annex, these mineral deposits transform the fossil into bands of black, blue, and silver stone. Like a storm frozen in stone. And imagine seeing this beast in the flesh!

2.name: Reginus Buca
2.description: Tales of some ancient seafarers, speak of beasts of this size rising from beneath the waves. The Sea Elves have their serpents, of course. Perhaps this is some scaley cousin to that Pyandonean stock?

3.name: Muzah-Tei
3.description: No, friend. See the ridge of bone above the brow. Poets would call it a dragon. It is a fish. But a fish unlike anything we see today, beyond excursions to Apocrphya.

1.name: Verita Numida
1.description: Early notes before my primary investigation. Thereâs quite the unique scale pattern on this scrollcase, and a curious amount of waterproofing material around the seams. Sea serpent scales, I believe? When I see sea serpents, I think Maormer.

2.name: Muzah-Tei
